edition.name: Migne PL 3 (1844), Epistola Firmiliani ad Cyprianum, via Corpus Corporum / Latin Wikisource
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Volo autem vobis et de historia quae apud nos facta est exponere ad hoc ipsum pertinente. Ante viginti enim et duos fere annos, temporibus post Alexandrum imperatorem, multae istic conflictationes et pressurae acciderunt, vel in commune omnibus hominibus, vel privatim Christianis, terrae etiam motus plurimi et frequentes exstiterunt, ut et per Cappadociam et per Pontum multa subruerent, quaedam etiam civitates, in profundum receptae, dirupti soli hiatu devorarentur, ut ex hoc persecutio quoque gravis adversum nos christiani nominis fieret, quae post longam retro aetatis pacem repente oborta de inopinato et insueto malo ad turbandum populum nostrum terribilior effecta est. Serenianus tunc fuit in nostra provincia praeses, acerbus et dirus persecutor. In hac autem perturbatione constitutis fidelibus, et huc atque illuc persecutionis metu fugientibus, et patrias suas relinquentibus, atque in alias partes regionum transeuntibus (erat enim transeundi facultas, eo quod persecutio illa, non per totum mundum, sed localis fuisset), emersit istic subito quaedam mulier, quae in extasim constituta propheten se praeferret et quasi sancto Spiritu plena sic ageret. Ita autem principalium daemoniorum impetu ferebatur, ut per longum tempus sollicitaret et deciperet fraternitatem, admirabilia quaedam et portentosa perficiens, et facere se terram moveri polliceretur. Non quod daemoni tanta esset potestas ut terram movere aut elementum concutere vi sua valeret, sed quod nonnumquam Spiritus nequam, praesciens et intelligens terrae motum futurum, id se facturum esse simularet quod futurum videret. Quibus mendaciis et jactationibus subegerat mentes singulorum ut sibi obedirent, et quocumque praeciperet et duceret sequerentur, faceret quoque mulierem illam cruda hyeme nudis pedibus per asperas nives ire nec vexari in aliquo aut laedi illa discursione, diceret etiam se in Judaeam et Hierosolymam festinare, fingens tamquam inde venisset. Hic et unum de presbyteris Rusticum, item et alium diaconum fefellit, ut eidem mulieri commiscerentur; quod paulo post detectum est: Nam subito apparuit illi unus de exorcistis vir probatus et circa religiosam disciplinam bene semper conversatus, qui exhortatione quoque fratrum plurimorum, qui et ipsi fortes ac laudabiles in fide aderant, excitatus, erexit se contra illum spiritum nequam revincendum; qui subtili fallacia etiam hoc paulo ante praedixerat, venturum quemdam adversum et tentatorem infidelem. Tamen ille exorcista, inspiratus, Dei gratia fortiter restitit, et esse illum nequissimum spiritum qui prius sanctus putabatur, ostendit. Atque illa mulier quae prius per praestigias et fallacias daemonis multa ad deceptionem fidelium moliebatur, inter caetera quibus plurimos deceperat, etiam hoc frequenter ausa est, ut et invocatione non contemptibili sanctificare se panem et Eucharistiam facere simularet, et sacrificium Domino sine sacramento solitae praedicationis offerret, baptizaret quoque multos usitata et legitima verba interrogationis usurpans, ut nil discrepare ab ecclesiastica regula videretur.
pass_a_gloss: I want to explain to you also the story that happened among us, pertaining to this very thing. For about twenty-two years ago, in the times after Emperor Alexander, many conflicts and pressures occurred, either in common to all people or privately to Christians, and many earthquakes and frequent ones existed, so that in Cappadocia and in Pontus many things were overthrown, and some cities, having been swallowed up into the depths, were devoured by the gaping earth, so that from this also a severe persecution against us of the Christian name was made, which after a long peace of the past age suddenly arose from an unexpected and unusual evil to disturb our people, made more terrifying. Serenianus was then the governor in our province, a harsh and dire persecutor. In this disturbance, with the faithful established and fleeing here and there in fear of persecution and leaving their homelands and crossing into other parts of the regions (for there was the ability to cross, because that persecution was not throughout the whole world but local), a certain woman suddenly emerged, who, having been placed in ecstasy, presented herself as a prophet and acted as if filled with the Holy Spirit. She was carried away by the impulse of principal demons, so that for a long time she disturbed and deceived the brotherhood, performing certain admirable and portentous things, and promising that she would make the earth move. Not that the demon had so much power that it could move the earth or shake an element by its own force, but that sometimes the evil Spirit, foreseeing and understanding the future earthquake, simulated that it would do what it saw was going to happen. By these lies and boasts, she had subjugated the minds of individuals so that they would obey her, and wherever she might command and lead, they would follow, and she even made herself, in the harsh winter, walk with bare feet through rough snow without being disturbed or harmed in any way by that walking, and she also said that she was hastening to Judea and Jerusalem, pretending as if she had come from there. Here, she also deceived one of the presbyters, Rusticus, and another deacon, so that they commingled with her; which was detected a little later: For suddenly one of the exorcists, a proven man who had always been well-conversant in religious discipline, appeared to her, who, having been exhorted also by the brothers, many of whom were strong and praiseworthy in faith, was stirred up and rose up against that evil spirit to overcome it; which, with subtle deceit, had even predicted a little before that an adversary and unfaithful tempter would come. Nevertheless, that exorcist, inspired by the grace of God, strongly withstood, and showed that it was a most evil spirit which was previously thought to be holy. And that woman, who previously, through the tricks and deceptions of the demon, had undertaken many things for the deception of the faithful, among other things by which she had deceived many, had also frequently dared to do this, that with a not contemptible invocation, she would simulate sanctifying bread and making the Eucharist, and would offer a sacrifice to the Lord without the sacrament of the usual preaching, and would also baptize many, using the usual and legitimate words of interrogation, so that nothing seemed to differ from the ecclesiastical rule.

pass_b_english: I also want to tell you about an episode in our own history that bears directly on this matter. About twenty-two years ago, after the reign of Emperor Alexander, our region was shaken by widespread unrest and heavy pressures that fell on everyone and on Christians in particular. Earthquakes struck repeatedly, toppling buildings throughout Cappadocia and Pontus and swallowing whole cities into gaping chasms. Out of that devastation a severe persecution broke out against us who bear the Christian name. After a long period of peace it erupted suddenly, an unexpected and unfamiliar evil that terrified our people all the more because it came without warning. Serenianus was governor of our province at the time, a harsh and ruthless persecutor.

In the midst of this turmoil the faithful held their ground, while many fled in fear from place to place, abandoned their homelands, and crossed into other regions; they could do so because the persecution was local, not empire-wide. Then a woman appeared suddenly. She claimed to be a prophet, threw herself into ecstatic trances, and acted as if she were filled with the Holy Spirit. In reality she was driven by the chief demons. For a long time she harassed and deceived the brotherhood, performing impressive and portentous signs and even promising to make the earth move. The demon did not actually have power to shake the ground or disturb the elements by its own force; rather, the evil spirit sometimes foresees a coming quake and then pretends to produce what it knows will happen anyway. By such lies and boasts she enslaved people's minds, so that they obeyed her and followed wherever she commanded and led. She even walked barefoot over rough snow in the bitter winter without harm or distress, and she announced she was hurrying to Judea and Jerusalem as if she had just come from there.

She deceived one of our presbyters, Rusticus, and a deacon as well, so that they became intimate with her. The fraud came to light not long after. A proven exorcist, a man of sound religious discipline, suddenly confronted her, stirred up by the encouragement of many brothers who were strong and commendable in faith. He stood up to overcome that evil spirit. The spirit had craftily predicted just before that an adversary and faithless tempter would come. Nevertheless, the exorcist, inspired by God's grace, resisted firmly and showed that the spirit once thought holy was in fact utterly wicked. The woman, who had previously used the demon's tricks and deceptions to mislead the faithful in many ways, had also repeatedly dared to simulate the consecration of bread and the celebration of the Eucharist with a solemn invocation, to offer a sacrifice to the Lord without the sacrament of the customary preaching, and to baptize many using the usual and legitimate words of interrogation, so that nothing appeared to differ from the church's rule.

review.notes: The Latin text is accurately translated in both Pass A and Pass B. The title 'Deception by a False Prophet' correctly captures the content. All key elements, including the historical context, the actions of the woman, the role of demons, and the exorcist's intervention, are preserved. The scripture citations are not applicable here, as no biblical text is quoted. The translation maintains the original meaning, including the distinction between the Holy Spirit and the evil spirit, and the use of appropriate terminology such as 'Dei gratia' for 'the grace of God'.
